claim: Small teams produce more disruptive work and large teams more developing work, per CD-index data: disruption falls 70% (papers), 30% (patents), 50% (software) from 1 to 50 members; solo authors are 72% more likely than 5-person teams to write a top-5% disruptive paper at equal hit rate. Verified in source text.
agent_test: Equal-token test: one agent with N diverse restarts then merge vs one deep chain; score novelty-rated outputs and accuracy.
audit_note: All CD-index figures come from one paper (Wu, Wang, Evans: arXiv and Nature versions, plus its SI); Milojevic 2015 measures cognitive extent, not disruption, so it does not independently confirm these numbers. The numbers themselves match the paper.

claim: About two thirds of the team-size/disruption effect remains when comparing the same author across their own papers (beta -0.00018 vs -0.00027, i.e. 67%); one third is sorting across scientists. Verified.
agent_test: Not testable on agents directly; use as caution that team size is confounded with task type.

claim: Larger teams get more citations on average, and authors per paper must keep rising to stay above world-average citation rate; sole-authored natural-science papers fell from 87% (1900) to 7% (2011).
agent_test: Background only.
audit_note: Larivière et al. is the main source for the 87% to 7% and rising-author-count points; Wu et al. only corroborates larger teams having more top-5% cited papers.

claim: Team size grows by roughly 13-18% per decade. Fortunato 2018 says 17% (citing Wuchty 2007 and Jones 2009) without years or base sizes. Wu 2019 SI gives papers 2 to 5.5 (1954-2014, about 18% per decade by our arithmetic) and patents 1.7 to 2.7 (about 13%); Jones 2009 gives patents 1.73 to 2.33 over 1975-1999 (about 13%). Team-authored share rose from about 50% (1955) to 90% (2013). The exact 17% is a review summary; Wuchty body text was not read.
agent_test: Background only.
audit_note: Fortunato's 17% per decade, the 50% (1955) to 90% (2013) team-authored share and Jones's 1.73 to 2.33 (1975-1999) all check; the Wu 2019 SI team-size figures (2 to 5.5 papers, 1.7 to 2.7 patents) were not in the main text I could open, but the 18% and 13% arithmetic from them is correct.

claim: Super ties (extreme-tail repeated coauthors) give a small productivity gain (about 5.2%, coefficient 0.11) and a 17% citation boost per paper; the 17% here is a citation figure, not team growth. The label depends on a tail-threshold assumption.
agent_test: Test fixed complementary role pairs (writer plus critic with persistent roles) vs fresh roles each call at equal tokens.

claim: Strong ties at country level raise productivity and citations, but a DBLP study finds weaker ties go with higher h-index among equally achieving scientists. The super-tie benefit is not settled.
agent_test: Background only.

claim: Remote teams are less disruptive than on-site teams across fields and sizes, but the controlled effect is small: P(D>0) 20.4% to 19.5% for papers and 58.2% to 56.5% for patents with full controls (raw 28% to 22% and 67% to 55%; percentile 89 to 84). New-concept probability 0.40% to 0.32%. Remote members take late technical tasks (conceiving 63% to 51% for the same scientists). No replication outside Wu's group found.
agent_test: Compare agents sharing full context vs summaries only; measure novelty.

claim: The decline in disruption over time (Park 2023) is largely an artefact: 972,161 papers and 142,362 patents have CD5=1; 97% of such papers and 78% of such patents list zero references; reanalysis negates (papers) or reduces (patents) the decline. Verified in source text.
agent_test: Background: warns that disruption metrics are fragile proxies.

claim: Multi-agent gains depend on task structure: +80.8% on decomposable finance (centralised) to -70.0% on sequential planning (independent); decentralised +9.2% on web navigation; all variants hurt on PlanCraft (-39% to -70%). Verified for Kim 2025.
schema_part: G9/O6 (decompose only when subtasks are independent)
agent_test: Equal-token: parallel subagents vs single chain on decomposable vs sequential tasks.
audit_note: All numbers come from Kim et al. (listed four times); MultiAgentBench and MacNet only corroborate that topology and agent count change results, not these figures.

claim: A capability ceiling exists: once the single agent exceeds about 0.45 raw performance, extra agents give negative returns (beta -0.236). The fit includes frontier models (GPT-5, Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro), and held-out frontier check on BrowseComp-Plus is MAE 0.061 (MAS-only), but authors call transfer preliminary. A separate Ringelmann study predicts c near 1 for high-accuracy frontier models, but ran no frontier team curve. Still one group per result.
agent_test: Measure when scaffold branching stops paying as base accuracy rises.

claim: Error amplification by topology: single 1.0, centralised 4.4, hybrid 5.1, decentralised 7.8, independent 17.2. A central verifier contains errors. Numbers verified.
agent_test: Compare independent parallel samples with no check vs sampling plus one verifier at equal tokens.

claim: Multi-agent debate does not reliably beat self-consistency or chain-of-thought at equal compute; original gains (Du 2023: GSM8K 77.0 to 85.0) shrink after tuning or stronger prompts.
agent_test: Equal-token: debate vs self-consistency vs single CoT on our benchmark.
audit_note: 'Shrink after tuning' should read: shrink once baselines (CoT, self-consistency) are tuned or strengthened; Smit et al. also report that tuning MAD's own agreement level can raise MAD accuracy. Du's GSM8K 77.0 to 85.0 matches (single agent vs debate).

claim: Simple sampling-and-voting gains rise with ensemble size (GSM8K +12 to 24 points, MATH +6 to 10), and sampling the best model repeatedly (Self-MoA) beats mixing models by 6.6 points AlpacaEval and 3.8% average. Verified in source.
agent_test: Compare N samples of one model with vote vs mixed-model ensemble at equal tokens.
audit_note: The paper says gains of '12% to 24%' on GSM8K and '6% to 10%' on MATH (accuracy gains, read as points); Self-MoA 6.6 AlpacaEval points and 3.8% average match.

claim: Model heterogeneity is contested but partly explained: Zhang 2025 beats the average of two similar models (GPT-4o-mini, Llama3.1-70b) by 6.4% (SoM) and 8.2% (EoT), while Li 2025 beats the best single model with Self-MoA (+6.6 AlpacaEval, +3.8 average). Li's fits show quality weighs more than diversity (e.g. MMLU 2.558 vs 1.841, R2 0.771) and diversity helps at fixed quality. Kim 2025 shows family-dependent results (Anthropic +31% with mixed orchestrator; OpenAI and Gemini degrade). Baselines differ (average vs best), so the conflict is mostly a quality-gap and baseline effect.
agent_test: Test prompt-role diversity vs model diversity at equal tokens.

claim: Failures of agent teams come mostly from design and coordination rather than model limits: MAST 14 modes, failure rate 41% to 86.7% across 7 frameworks; shares 44.2% design, 32.3% misalignment, 23.5% verification; kappa 0.88. Verified.
agent_test: Audit our agent traces with MAST categories.
audit_note: Rests on the MAST paper alone (listed twice); Mieczkowski is unrelated to the MAST numbers. Paper concedes some failures stem from LLM limits but argues they are not merely model-driven; category shares 44.2/32.3/23.5 appear in its table.

claim: Fixing roles and workflow gives modest gains: ChatDev +9.4% from better role specification alone and +15.6% (maximum) from adding a high-level task-objective verification step, same model (Cemri v3). Failures not removed. Category shares are inconsistent inside the paper (44.2/32.3/23.5 vs 41.8/36.9/21.3).
agent_test: Ablate explicit role text at equal tokens.

claim: Coordination cost is real: Amdahl bound is not reached even on parallel tasks (median 2.19x), self-coordinated teams send more messages and duplicate claims.
agent_test: Count duplicated work in parallel subagents with and without pre-assignment.
audit_note: Median 2.19x, H=61.4 and message-count result verified in Mieczkowski PDF; note Claude Sonnet 4.6 alone did not plateau below the bound (p=0.45). Kim paper not needed for this claim.

claim: Homogeneous debating LLM teams hit a hard ceiling: effective team size 1/c about 1.2 to 1.8; 30 debaters add no diversity vs 1 on MMLU-Hard; each extra member cut odds of success about 8% (OR 0.92) in a separate grid. Directional agreement from two 2026 preprints; not peer reviewed.
agent_test: Check answer diversity vs N at equal tokens.
audit_note: Verified Bertalanic and Fortuna (ceilings 1.2/1.8/1.2, N=30 no more diversity than 1 on MMLU-Hard) and Riedl (7,150 runs, OR 0.92, GPT-4.1); Riedl arXiv is 2025 (v4 2026).

claim: Weaker agents conform to wrong feedback: about 10% of MGSM errors were a correct GPT-3.5 agent talked out of its answer; not seen with GPT-4; conformity helps only if agents lean right.
agent_test: Inject wrong feedback to the agent and measure flip rate.
audit_note: AgentVerse (~10% of MGSM errors, absent with GPT-4) verified; the two AgentVerse entries are the same paper; Zhang et al. shows conformity is beneficial or harmful depending on whether right answers dominate (helps on ChatGPT/Qwen-72B, harms on Llama2).

claim: Network topology matters but no topology wins on every task; irregular random graphs best on average in MacNet (0.6522 vs CoT 0.5757), with a logistic scaling curve; Kim finds centralised more error-safe.
agent_test: Background.

claim: AI-using scientists gain personally while science narrows. Multipliers confirmed in the arXiv v4 text: 3.02x papers, 4.84x citations, 1.37 years earlier to lead, topics shrink 4.63%. After matching on early trajectory the gain is smaller: +24.45% citations and +9.61% productivity at career year 10. AI teams are 19.29% smaller (juniors 2.89 to 1.99). Observational, one group.
agent_test: Measure diversity of ideas from our agent with vs without a retrieval tool.

claim: Research-agent systems that run generate-debate-rank loops improve with test-time compute (Elo up across ten buckets; top answer GPQA 78.4%); human co-pilot checkpoints help clarity but lower significance (-0.3).
agent_test: Equal-token tournament vs best-of-N.

claim: Team diversity raises paper and citation counts but lowers satisfaction and perceived effectiveness (22 working groups, mixed methods).
agent_test: Background.

claim: No independent replication of Wu 2019 was found and nobody has rerun it with zero-reference entries removed (Holst 2024 does not test team size). Wu's SI shows robustness to author fixed effects, topic and journal controls, and reference-based measures, which lowers but does not remove the risk. Lin 2023 points the same way but is from the same group. No LLM study tests 17%/decade growth or complementary super-ties directly.
agent_test: Gap.

claim: Vertical structure (one solver, reviewers refine) suits maths and software; horizontal suits consultancy-style tasks.
agent_test: Compare solver-plus-reviewer to parallel peers on maths at equal tokens.

claim: The 17% per decade team-growth figure is a review summary, and the same review uses 17% for a different effect (17% more citations for publications with extremely strong collaborators, Petersen 2015). Do not conflate them.
agent_test: Background only.
audit_note: Fortunato 2018 text states 17% per decade (refs 50, 54) and 17% more citations for extremely strong collaborators (ref 59 Petersen 2015); Petersen abstract reports the 17% apostle effect.

claim: Mixing models in LLM teams helps mainly when the models are close in quality. Quality has a larger coefficient than diversity in MoA fits (R2 0.69-0.77), and in-model sampling of the best model beats cross-model mixing. This supports restarts of one strong model over mixing in a single-agent scaffold.
agent_test: At equal tokens: N restarts of the best model plus merge vs mixed weaker models.

claim: Several MAST failure modes (step repetition, unaware of termination, premature termination, no or incorrect verification) do not need a second agent and can arise in one agent's own chain; adding an external task-objective verification step gave the largest measured gain (+15.6%). No study has coded single-agent scaffold traces with MAST.
agent_test: Code our own traces with MAST modes 1.3, 1.5, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3; add stop and verify rules; compare.

claim: AI adoption is associated with smaller teams (19.29% fewer authors; juniors -31.14%), so tools may substitute for headcount; matched-cohort gains are tens of percent, not multiples.
agent_test: Background only.
